blocks.text: Drink a litre of water on a cool morning and within an hour you need the toilet. Spend the same hour weeding a farm under the Kano sun and you may pass no urine at all, though you drank the same litre. Your kidneys made that decision without consulting you.

blocks.markdown:
## The kidney and the nephron

Each kidney is a bean-shaped organ about 11 cm long, receiving blood through the **renal artery** and returning it through the **renal vein**. Inside, three zones can be recognised: the outer **cortex**, the inner **medulla**, and a funnel-shaped space, the **pelvis**, that drains into the **ureter**.

Each kidney contains about a million microscopic filtering units called **nephrons**. Picture a single nephron: a knot of capillaries, the **glomerulus**, sits inside a cup called the **Bowmans capsule** in the cortex. From the cup runs a tubule — first the coiled **proximal convoluted tubule**, then a long hairpin, the **loop of Henle**, dipping into the medulla, then the **distal convoluted tubule**, and finally the **collecting duct**, which carries urine to the pelvis. Blood capillaries wrap tightly around the whole tubule along its entire length.

blocks.title: How urine is made
blocks.prompt: Describe how blood entering the kidney is converted into urine, naming the two main processes.

steps.text: Ultrafiltration. Blood arrives in the glomerulus through a wide arteriole and leaves through a narrower one, which raises the pressure inside. This pressure forces water and all small dissolved molecules out through the capillary wall into the Bowmans capsule.

What passes and what does not. Water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts, urea and vitamins pass through. Blood cells and plasma proteins are too large and stay in the blood. The liquid formed is the glomerular filtrate.

Selective reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Useful substances are taken back into the surrounding capillaries: all the glucose and amino acids by active transport, most mineral salts, and much of the water by osmosis. Because the process is selective, urea is left behind.

Water conservation. The loop of Henle sets up a salty environment in the medulla, so as the fluid flows down the collecting duct through this region, water is drawn out of it by osmosis and the urine becomes concentrated.
The result. What remains — mainly water, urea and excess salts — is urine. It flows to the pelvis, down the ureter to the bladder, and out through the urethra.

blocks.answer: Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus removes all small molecules from the blood; selective reabsorption along the tubule returns the useful ones. What is left behind — water, urea and excess salts — is urine.

blocks.title: Homeostasis
blocks.text: The maintenance of a constant internal environment despite changes outside the body. Blood glucose, water content, salt concentration, temperature and pH are all held within narrow limits, because the enzymes that run the body only work properly within those limits.

blocks.markdown:
### Osmoregulation: controlling the water content of blood

The control is by **negative feedback** — the response cancels out the change that caused it.

If blood becomes **too concentrated** (after sweating, or eating salty food), receptors in the hypothalamus detect it. The pituitary gland releases more **ADH** (antidiuretic hormone). ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood. The urine produced is small in volume and dark, and the blood returns to normal.

If blood becomes **too dilute** (after drinking a lot of water), less ADH is released. The collecting ducts become less permeable, less water is reabsorbed, and a large volume of pale, dilute urine is passed.

This is why the same litre of water has such different effects on a cool day and on a hot farm: when you are sweating heavily, ADH output is high and the kidney holds onto almost every drop.

### Temperature regulation

Humans are **homoiothermic** (warm-blooded) and hold body temperature near 37 °C.

When the body is **too hot**: sweat glands secrete more sweat, and evaporation of that water absorbs latent heat from the skin. Arterioles in the skin dilate (**vasodilation**) so more warm blood flows near the surface and loses heat by radiation. Hair lies flat and the person is less active.

When the body is **too cold**: sweating stops, skin arterioles constrict (**vasoconstriction**) to keep warm blood deep in the body, hair stands erect to trap a layer of insulating air, and shivering — rapid involuntary muscle contraction — generates heat by respiration.

blocks.title: Glucose in urine
blocks.text: A healthy nephron reabsorbs all the filtered glucose in the proximal tubule, so urine should contain none. Glucose in the urine indicates diabetes mellitus: blood glucose is so high that the filtered load exceeds what the carrier proteins can reabsorb.

blocks.title: Get the ADH direction right
blocks.text: More ADH means more water reabsorbed and less urine. The name helps: antidiuretic means against urine production. Candidates who reverse this lose every mark in the question.

Selective reabsorption returns all glucose and amino acids, most salts and much water to the blood, leaving urea behind.
Homeostasis keeps the internal environment constant so that enzymes can function.
More ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and less urine is produced.
The body cools itself by sweating and vasodilation, and warms itself by shivering and vasoconstriction.
